title: King of Kelewele
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Hwentia, anise seed, cloves and a great deal of ginger blended with water, the fibres squeezed out, and only the liquid used to coat the plantain.
longDesc: Kelewele is spiced fried plantain and it is the best street snack in Ghana. This version is the most heavily spiced documented anywhere: two to four ounces of fresh ginger, a teaspoon of anise seed, a teaspoon of whole cloves, three or four sticks of hwentia and a couple of tablespoons of onion, blended with two or three tablespoons of water. The trick she arrived at on her third attempt is the useful part — squeeze out the coarse fibres and use only the liquid to coat the plantain. Four slightly over-ripe plantains, cubed, rested a few minutes, fried at about 350 degrees Fahrenheit.
ingredients: Fresh habanero or red pepper, to taste — start with about 1/2 tsp
About 1/4 tsp salt, or more to taste
equipment: Sieve or cloth, for squeezing out the fibres
steps: Blend the onion, ginger, pepper and hwentia with 2 or 3 tablespoons of water.
Squeeze out the fibrous strings and keep mostly the liquid.
Stir in the anise seed, cloves, salt and the optional nutmeg.
Coat them with a few tablespoons of the seasoning liquid.
Heat the oil to about 350 degrees Fahrenheit.
Fry in batches until nicely browned on all sides.
Remove and drain on paper towels. Best eaten immediately or soon after cooking.
chefTips: Squeeze out the fibres and use the liquid. Her own account is that she tried it three times and this worked best — the coarse ginger and hwentia strings do not want to be in the finished dish.
Her ripeness note is the key to kelewele: part of the secret is having the plantains ripe enough, so the sweetness comes through and they caramelise on the outside.
Slightly over-ripe, not merely ripe. Too firm and it will not caramelise; too soft and it absorbs oil.
Hwentia is grains of selim, the smoky West African pepper pod — three or four sticks is a lot and it is what makes this version taste of itself.
350 degrees Fahrenheit, which is one of only two documented frying temperatures for this dish with a stated unit. The other named sources give 180 degrees Celsius, which is the same thing.
Fry in batches and do not crowd the pan. Crowded plantain steams rather than fries.
Traditionally served with bean stew, though she prefers dry-roasted peanuts. Groundnuts are the usual street pairing.
commonMistakes: Leaving the fibres in the marinade.
Under-ripe plantain, which will not caramelise.
Skipping the hwentia, which is the whole character.
Letting it stand long after frying — it goes soft fast.
sources: Adapted from 'King of Kelewele (Recipe #53)', betumiblog.blogspot.com, timestamped 2011-06-19. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 6:44 PM'. NO YIELD is printed; the four servings above follows from four plantains and is editorial.

Ingredients exactly as printed, TWO-PASS: '2 to 4 oz' fresh ginger; 'a teaspoon of anise seed'; 'about 1/4 teaspoon salt (or more to taste)'; '1 teaspoon whole cloves'; 'about 1/4 teaspoon nutmeg (optional)'; '3 or 4 sticks hwentia'; 'a couple of tablespoons' of onion; fresh habanero or red pepper 'to taste'; '4 slightly over-ripe plantains'; oil for deep frying. SINGLE-PASS: start the pepper at about half a teaspoon, and blend with '2 or 3 tablespoons of water'.
NOTE THE RANGE ON GINGER: '2 to 4 oz' is a twofold spread in the dominant spice, printed as such and not narrowed.

Method as printed: blend onion, ginger, pepper and hwentia with water, remove the fibrous strings, and use mostly the liquid; cube the plantains and coat with a few tablespoons of the seasoning; rest several minutes; oil 'to about 350 degrees F' (TWO-PASS); fry in batches.
DONENESS CUE, verbatim and TWO-PASS: 'When they are nicely browned on all sides, remove and drain them on paper towels.' And: 'They're best eaten immediately or soon after cooking.'
THE TECHNIQUE SHE ARRIVED AT BY TRIAL, verbatim: 'The third time I squeezed out the coarse fibers and just used some of the liquid to coat the plantains, and this seemed to work best.'

THE RIPENESS RULE, verbatim: 'Part of the secret in making good kelewele is having the plantains ripe enough, so the sweetness comes through and they kind of carmellize on the outside.' — spelling as printed.

PROVENANCE AND DEDICATION: the post is dedicated to her son-in-law Koranteng and opens 'Today is my son-in-law's first official Father's Day (his Kumiwah is 3+ months old), and this post is dedicated to him.' SINGLE-PASS: she mentions 'Maame's' spice mix and Barbara Baeta's test kitchen.
SERVING, as printed: traditionally served with bean stew; she prefers dry-roasted peanuts.

FIVE NAMED SOURCES AND NO SHARED SPICE SYSTEM, recorded unreconciled. (1) This version: ginger, anise, cloves, hwentia, nutmeg. (2) Fafa Gilbert (GHA050): aniseed, calabash nutmeg or allspice pods, cloves, black peppercorns. (3) Demand Africa, byline the site's own name, 3 May 2017, TWO-PASS: only '1-2 tsp Cayenne pepper or ½ teaspoon of red-pepper', '½ tsp peeled grated fresh gingerroot', '1 tsp salt', '2 tbs water' for '4-6 plantains' — no warm spices at all. (4) The Storied Recipe, byline 'admin' on one fetch and 'Recipe from podcast guest Adjwoa' on another, 8 servings: 6 ripe plantains, ½ cup water, 1 onion, 1 tbsp cayenne, a fist-sized root of ginger, 1 tsp salt. (5) A PBS subdomain page bylined 'by Marcus Samuelsson on Jan 14, 2020', with 'recipe courtesy of Ope Amosu' appearing on one fetch only: 4 plantains, ¼ red onion, 2 tbsp ginger, 2 tsp garlic, 2 tsp cayenne, 1½ tsp lemon juice, 1½ tsp chicken bouillon, 1 tsp salt, ½ tsp nutmeg, with a 45-to-90-minute refrigerated marinade. NO TWO AGREE ON SPICE QUANTITIES and the plantain counts run 2, 4-6, 6 and unstated.

FRYING TEMPERATURE ACROSS SOURCES: 'about 350 degrees F' here; '350 degrees' with NO UNIT at Demand Africa; '360°F / 180°C' at The Storied Recipe, which adds a thermometer-free test — 'heat until there are slight ripples across the top of the oil'; 'around 180 degrees Celsius' in the Ghanaian Times; and no temperature at all on the PBS-subdomain page.

NAME AND ORIGIN, from Regina Benneh, Ghanaian Times, no date, TWO-PASS: 'Kelewele grew out of everyday cooking in southern Ghana, especially among the people of the Ga and Akan tribes, very common on the streets of Accra, Kumasi, and Cape Coast.' Her etymology, offered as hers: "The name 'Kelewele' is a Ga dialect and combination of 'Kele' (cut into small pieces) and 'Wele' (fried)." That is the basis for the community attribution above.

A HISTORICAL NOTE from Whitby 1968, a CSIR Food Research Institute bulletin: plantain 'fried in oil--either in large pieces or in half-inch cubes, seasoned with ginger. This form, called kelewele is commoner along the coast.' Note that in 1968 the documented seasoning was ginger alone.

A SOURCE FLAGGED AND NOT USED FOR QUANTITIES: a page on weeatatlast.com bylined 'Kate Hahnel', 30 November 2025, 8 servings. Site ownership and the byline could not be confirmed, its peppers and calabash nutmeg carry no quantities, and its 'mixed spice' is unspecified. Its useful SINGLE-PASS notes are recorded: let the plantain sit in the seasoning 5-10 minutes, use moderately ripe fruit since oversoft ones absorb excess oil, and do not overcrowd.
storage: Eat at once. Kelewele does not keep.
reheating: A hot oven briefly, at a push. Never the microwave.
healthBenefits: Ripe plantain is high in potassium, vitamin A and vitamin B6.
Ginger, cloves and selim all carry documented antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory compounds.
Served with groundnuts it becomes a reasonably complete snack.
culturalNote: Kelewele is sold in paper cones from braziers after dark in Accra, with a twist of roasted groundnuts on top, and it is the thing people miss most when they leave Ghana. That the 1968 government record describes it seasoned with ginger alone, while modern recipes pile in cloves, anise, nutmeg and selim, is a nice record of a street food getting more elaborate over sixty years.
